the ship believing it will survive the *next* storm specifically because it survived the last, they have committed the inductive fallacy Popper rejects.","If the structural integrity of the ship can be probabilistically calculated from past stress, the analogy breaks as science (for Popper) allows no such calculation."],"shared_structure":["Selection based on survival of severe stress tests","No guarantee of future survival despite past success","Preference for the option with highest demonstrated resilience"],"source_memory_refs":["naval_strategy_severe_weather"],"transfer_claims":["Just as a captain chooses the ship that survived the hurricane not because it is 'unsinkable' but because it is the only one known to be floating, a scientist chooses the corroborated theory because it is the only one not known to be false."]},"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms as a non-inductive 'critical preference' grounded in the methodological aim of truth-likeness (verisimilitude), but accepting this costs the agent any rational assurance that the preferred theory will succeed in future applications, rendering the preference purely procedural rather than predictive.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If verisimilitude cannot be formally defined without collapsing into probabilistic induction (as later proved by Tich\u00fd and induction is merely semantic.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If scientists actually rely on an implicit uniformity principle when choosing theories, Popper's description of their rationality is empirically false.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'inductive inference' (claiming past success increases future probability) and 'critical preference' (selecting the theory that has withstood the most severe tests as the best current candidate for truth, while explicitly acknowledging it may fail tomorrow). This relies on Popper's concept of verisimilitude: we prefer Theory A over B not because A is more likely true, but because A has higher content and has survived tests that falsified B or competitors, making it logically closer to the truth *so far*, without implying it will remain so.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
